story.title: Increase daily payment limits for premium customers
story.description: Increase daily payment limits for premium customers from AED 25,000 to AED 50,000 for domestic transfers. The payment-service must obtain premium eligibility and the effective account limit from account-service before accepting each payment. Keep fraud screening active through fraud-engine and use the transaction ledger in transaction-db to calculate the remaining daily allowance, including concurrent requests. Roll out the business rule behind an approved feature flag during the payments release window. Operations must confirm threshold monitoring and rollback readiness before enabling the higher limit; standard customer limits remain unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: A premium account can submit domestic payments totaling AED 50,000 per bank-local calendar day; the next payment is declined.
A standard account retains its AED 25,000 daily limit and existing per-payment checks.
Concurrent payment submissions cannot exceed the account daily limit, and retries create one transaction ledger posting.
Every accepted payment passes fraud screening; operations approves monitoring and can restore the previous limit with the feature flag.

requirement.business_summary: Increase daily payment limit for premium customers from AED 25,000 to AED 50,000 for domestic transfers while keeping standard customer limits unchanged.

The change is gated by a feature flag; operations will monitor and can rollback via the flag.
requirement.engineering_scope: Update payment-service to query account-service for premium eligibility and dynamic daily limit, integrate with fraud-engine, use transaction-db for daily allowance calculation with concurrency handling, introduce feature flag for rollout, and adjust monitoring/rollback procedures.

tests.summary: Selected 15 catalog tests and 8 new tests, covering 15 of 17 impacted nodes (88%); estimated effort is 13.2 hours.

frameworks.reason: PII-bearing components are impacted; the change touches customer data.

findings.text: The change makes payment-service request premium status and an effective daily limit from account-service before accepting a payment, so customer attributes are newly used inside the payment authorization decision. The purpose limitation, minimization and retention basis for that eligibility lookup, and for the profile attributes read from customer-db, should be confirmed before rollout.

Personal data traverses api-gateway and authentication-service on the same path as the new limit check, including token scope and session context. Exposure of eligibility or limit attributes in gateway logs, traces and error responses, and the scope checks enforced at authentication-service, should be reviewed.

Limit-change communications routed through notification-service rely on consent-aware delivery to verified destinations. The content of those messages, the preference lookup against customer-db, and any change in notification volume triggered by the new limit should be checked for data minimization and consent coverage.

recommendations: Confirm lawful basis, purpose limitation, minimization and retention for the premium-eligibility and effective-limit data exchanged between payment-service and account-service, including attributes sourced from customer-db.
Verify that access controls, token scopes and logging on api-gateway and authentication-service cover the new limit-check path and do not surface personal data in logs or error payloads.
Review consent and channel preferences in notification-service before any limit-change messaging, and confirm privacy regression tests exist for the affected flow.

frameworks.reason: card-data components are impacted.

findings.text: The change does not introduce card data into the payment limit flow, but fraud-engine is a shared screening component also used for card-not-present velocity checks. Any rule, configuration or data-flow change on that component should be assessed for its effect on the cardholder data environment, segmentation and logging.

card-service and api-gateway handle card lifecycle and card status routing adjacent to the modified payment path. Payloads, routing rules and step-up calls should be checked to confirm no cardholder data is added to the new limit-enforcement request or response chain, including calls through authentication-service.

recommendations: Confirm that no cardholder data elements are introduced into the new premium-eligibility or daily-limit payloads exchanged between payment-service, account-service and transaction-db.
Review fraud-engine rule and configuration changes for impact on card-not-present velocity screening and confirm card-data security tests still exercise the affected screening path.
Re-verify masking, encryption and access restrictions on card-service and its routing through api-gateway and authentication-service after the limit change is deployed.

frameworks.reason: financial-data components are impacted; audit-data components are impacted; the change touches financial data.

findings.text: The change alters payment authorization logic in payment-service using a premium eligibility result from account-service, which affects how financial transactions are accepted and against what limit. This is a business-rule change on a financially significant path and requires change-management evidence, control-owner approval and testing before release.

Daily allowance is computed from transaction-db with concurrency handling, so posting accuracy, idempotency and daily-total consistency are exposed. Reconciliation of ledger entries and daily totals should be performed to confirm the new calculation does not create duplicate, missing or misstated postings.

Limit decisions and eligibility outcomes should remain traceable through audit-db, with downstream effect on reporting-db projections and risk-engine and fraud-engine signals. Completeness, immutability and retention of the audit records supporting the changed rule should be verified.

recommendations: Reconcile transaction-db ledger entries and daily totals after the change, and verify idempotent posting behaviour under concurrent payment requests.
Document control-owner approval, test evidence and rollback criteria for the payment limit business-rule change in payment-service and account-service.
Verify that audit-db events for limit and eligibility decisions are complete and append-only, and confirm reporting-db projections reflect the revised limit behaviour.

frameworks.reason: directly changed components have criticality >= 8.

findings.text: Directly changed components include payment-service, account-service, fraud-engine and transaction-db, which are high-criticality services on tier1 paths with wide downstream dependency. Service-owner approval, documented rollback criteria and release evidence should be in place before the change is promoted.

The rollout depends on a feature flag as the primary control gate. Flag ownership, default state, evaluation scope and a defined sunset should be recorded so the flag cannot be used to bypass limit enforcement or persist untracked after rollout.

Concurrency handling for daily allowance and monitoring/rollback procedures are part of the engineering scope, but observability coverage across the affected services and their downstream ledger writes should be checked. Authorization tests and operational monitoring evidence will be needed to demonstrate the change behaves as intended.

recommendations: Obtain service-owner approval and record the rollback plan for payment-service, account-service, fraud-engine and transaction-db before promotion.
Define feature-flag ownership, safe default, evaluation scope and sunset date, and confirm the flag cannot bypass limit enforcement once disabled.
Verify authorization tests, concurrency handling and operational monitoring for the affected path, and retain release evidence covering api-gateway and authentication-service interactions.

story.title: Customer profile: add preferred name and secondary email
story.description: Extend the customer profile with an optional preferred name and secondary email for service notifications. The customer-service stores this personal data in customer-db through a backward-compatible schema change and synchronizes the contact projection with CRM. The notification-service may use the secondary email only after verification and explicit customer consent. Keep the legal name and primary email behavior unchanged, including customers who leave the new fields blank. Apply existing retention, access, correction and erasure controls to both fields, and record the consent evidence needed for GDPR review.
acceptance_criteria: Preferred name accepts 1-80 characters and is optional; the legal name remains unchanged.
Secondary email must have valid email syntax and complete verification before notification delivery is enabled.
Customer profile updates persist in customer-db and synchronize with CRM without overwriting the primary email.
Withdrawal of consent stops secondary email notifications, and access or erasure requests include both new personal data fields.

findings.text: The change adds preferred_name and secondary_email fields to the customer profile system of record, expanding the personal data held in customer-service and customer-db. Verification and consent flags used by notification-service introduce a new processing purpose for secondary email contact data, and consent evidence handling needs to be confirmed before the field is used for notifications.

Synchronizing the new fields into the CRM contact projection extends the population of records in scope for access, correction, erasure and consent-withdrawal handling downstream of the system of record.

recommendations: Confirm lawful basis, stated purpose, retention and erasure handling for preferred_name and secondary_email across customer-service, customer-db, crm and notification-service.
Verify consent capture, evidence retention and withdrawal propagation before notification-service is permitted to use the secondary email, including preferences surfacing through crm.
Review profile read paths through api-gateway and authentication-service to confirm the new fields are scoped, minimized or masked appropriately for each caller.
Confirm subject access, correction and erasure flows cover the new fields and that audit-db logging for profile changes is consistent with existing retention controls.

frameworks.reason: card-data components are impacted.

findings.text: The change does not touch card data directly, but card-service shares customer-db, api-gateway and authentication-service with the profile flow, so the exposure is whether new profile fields can enter card-data request or response paths.
Identity and gateway paths carry both card and profile traffic; ignored or widened token scope, masking or step-up behavior on these shared components would be the exposure area requiring check.
New profile change events will be written alongside cardholder-related access records in audit-db, so integrity, append-only behavior and retention consistency require confirmation.

recommendations: Confirm no cardholder data fields or card-service payloads are extended by the profile change, and verify masking remains enforced in card-service and api-gateway responses.

Audit-db is an append-only store with integrity and retention controls, so new profile change events should be confirmed as not affecting the immutability or queryability of financial audit records.

story.title: Card freeze/unfreeze in mobile app with step-up authentication
story.description: Add card freeze/unfreeze controls to the mobile app through a new API gateway endpoint backed by card-service. Each card status change requires step-up authentication from authentication-service, binds the proof to the device and requested action, and exposes only masked card details. Update mobile-banking and api-gateway authorization policies together with the card control flow. PCI DSS review and security sign-off are outstanding: the prototype permits cross-device proof replay and lacks fail-closed verification evidence. These unresolved authentication defects and the missing rollback rehearsal are release blockers until the acceptance criteria have demonstrated evidence.
acceptance_criteria: A cardholder can freeze or unfreeze their own card in mobile-banking through the API gateway endpoint, and the refreshed view shows the confirmed status.
Each action requires a fresh step-up proof bound to the card, device and requested action; replay and cross-customer requests are rejected.
If authentication-service is unavailable or proof validation fails, card-service leaves the card status unchanged and denies the action.
Card control traces contain masked identifiers only; PCI DSS review, security sign-off and a rehearsed rollback are mandatory before release.

requirement.business_summary: Adds card freeze/unfreeze functionality to the mobile banking app, requiring step-up authentication and exposing only masked card details via a new API gateway endpoint backed by the card service.
requirement.technical_summary: Introduces a new REST endpoint in the API gateway that calls the card-service to update card status; each request mandates fresh step-up authentication from the authentication-service bound to device, card and action; mobile-banking UI and gateway authorization policies are updated to invoke the endpoint; responses return masked card identifiers only; card-service retains current status on auth failure or unavailability.
requirement.engineering_scope: Implement new API gateway endpoint for card freeze/unfreeze, integrate with card-service to update card status, add step-up authentication flow with authentication-service binding proof to device, card and action, update mobile-banking UI and API gateway authorization policies, ensure only masked card data is exposed, complete PCI DSS review and security sign-off, and rehearse rollback procedures.

findings.text: The new card freeze/unfreeze capability routes customer- and account-linked requests through the mobile channel, the external gateway and an identity step-up challenge, so personal data processing exposure extends across the mobile banking surface, gateway routing layer, authentication service and card service as a result of this change.

Although responses are described as returning masked card identifiers only, the device-, card- and action-bound step-up proof introduces additional authentication and device-identifying artefacts whose minimisation, purpose limitation and retention characteristics require assessment alongside existing identity data held for the authentication service and card service.

Indirect exposure may reach customer profile, contact preference and notification components if card status changes trigger servicing updates or customer messaging through gateway-routed calls, warranting checks that the change does not widen the data reaching the customer service, customer database, CRM or notification service beyond their existing declared purposes.

recommendations: Assess and document data minimisation, purpose and retention for the personal data and step-up authentication artefacts handled by mobile-banking, api-gateway, authentication-service and card-service, and confirm the records of processing reflect the new card status journey.

Modification of the authentication flow to require fresh step-up proof bound to device, card and action raises exposure around token issuance, scope validation and privileged action authorisation, requiring review of the authentication service and gateway policy enforcement points.

Because the change touches card-related components, the controls around card data encryption, masking and role-based access restrictions warrant re-verification across the card service, gateway, identity layer, ATM channel and fraud screening components that interact with card activity.

story.title: Fraud rule update: velocity check for card-not-present payments
story.description: Update the fraud rule in fraud-engine to add a rolling velocity check for card-not-present payments. The payment-service must supply the existing payment event attributes and apply the returned screening decision before posting. The risk engine provides the current policy signal used when the threshold is exceeded. Block the sixth attempt for the same card token within a rolling sixty-second window, including declined attempts. This change shares the payment screening path and core-payments deployment with ST-101, so both stories must agree on rule ordering, combined regression coverage and rollout timing.
acceptance_criteria: The first five card-not-present attempts for one card token inside sixty seconds are evaluated normally; the sixth is blocked by the velocity rule.
Declined attempts count toward the velocity window, while distinct card tokens maintain independent counters.
fraud-engine includes the active risk-engine policy signal and rule version in its screening decision.
Combined ST-101 and ST-110 regression evidence confirms premium payment limits cannot bypass fraud screening; their core-payments release order is agreed.

requirement.business_summary: Fraud rule update to block card-not-present payment attempts once a single card token reaches the sixth attempt within a rolling sixty-second window. The first five attempts are evaluated normally; the sixth is blocked by the new velocity rule. Declined attempts count toward the window, and separate card tokens keep independent counters. The rule change is delivered together with ST-101 on the shared payment screening path and core-payments deployment, so rule ordering, combined regression evidence and release timing must be agreed between both stories, and the combined evidence must confirm premium payment limits cannot bypass fraud screening.
requirement.technical_summary: A rolling velocity check is added to the fraud rule in fraud-engine for card-not-present payments, keyed by card token over a sixty-second window, inclusive of declined attempts. payment-service continues to supply the existing payment event attributes and must apply the returned screening decision before posting. The screening decision returned by fraud-engine is extended to include the active risk-engine policy signal and the rule version. The change shares the payment screening path and core-payments deployment with ST-101, requiring agreed rule ordering, combined ST-101 and ST-110 regression coverage and an agreed release order.

Submit a payment request through payment-service.
Observe that payment-service waits for the fraud-engine screening decision.
If the decision is APPROVE, payment-service posts a ledger entry to transaction-db; if BLOCK, it aborts posting.
Audit-db receives an audit event containing the decision, rule version, and correlation identifier.
tests.expected: For an APPROVE decision, a ledger entry is created and the audit event records APPROVE; for a BLOCK decision, no ledger entry is posted and the audit event records BLOCK with the associated rule version and policy signal.

tests.title: Operational: Ensure downstream services receive fraud decline notifications for blocked sixth CNP attempt
steps: Trigger a sixth CNP attempt that is blocked by the velocity rule.
Payment-service returns a decline to the caller and publishes a fraud decline event.
Account-service consumes the event, logs it, and leaves the available balance unchanged.
Notification-service consumes the event and sends a fraud alert to the customer via their registered channel.
tests.expected: Account-service balance shows no change and logs the decline event; Notification-service delivers a fraud alert; both services include the correlation identifier in their logs.

tests.title: Delivery: Verify coordinated release of fraud-engine and payment-service with ST-101 includes matching rule versions
steps: Deploy ST-101 and ST-110 together in a staging environment.
Query fraud-engine for the active rule version via GET /fraud/rules/{id}.
Execute a test CNP payment through payment-service and capture the screening decision returned.
Confirm that the rule version in the decision matches the version queried from fraud-engine and that the decision includes the current risk-engine policy signal.
tests.expected: The rule version from fraud-engine and the version embedded in payment-service's screening decision are identical, and the decision contains the active risk-engine policy signal, indicating a coordinated release.

tests.title: Operational: Confirm risk-engine supplies current policy signal when velocity threshold exceeded and fraud-engine includes it in decision
steps: Ensure risk-engine has an active policy identified as POL-2025-V1 loaded.
Generate six CNP attempts for the same card token within a sixty-second window (the sixth should trigger the velocity rule).
Invoke the fraud-engine screening endpoint for the sixth attempt.
Inspect the returned screening decision for the policySignal field.
tests.expected: The screening decision includes policySignal = POL-2025-V1, the correct rule version, and a BLOCK action, showing that risk-engine's signal is properly propagated.

tests.title: Delivery: Clarify medium ambiguity by validating velocity rule counts declined attempts and resets after sixty-second window
steps: Send five declined CNP payment attempts for a specific card token within a forty-second window.
Wait twenty-five seconds so that the sliding window now exceeds sixty seconds from the first attempt.
Submit a new CNP payment attempt (should be the first in the new window).
Observe the fraud-engine screening decision for this attempt.
tests.expected: After the window exceeds sixty seconds, the attempt counter resets; the new attempt is evaluated as the first attempt and is approved (assuming no other blocks). The five prior declined attempts are confirmed to have been counted within the original window.

tests.title: Operational: Assess payment-service latency SLA remains under threshold when fraud velocity rule active under load
steps: Execute a load test with 100 concurrent CNP payment requests, where approximately 50% are configured to trigger the sixth-attempt block.
Measure the average response time from payment-service receipt of request to return of the screening decision.
Verify that all responses are returned within the agreed SLA (e.g., 200 ms) and that no requests time out.
tests.expected: Average latency stays below the SLA threshold, all responses include the correct screening decision (APPROVE or BLOCK as appropriate), and the system remains stable without errors or timeouts.

story.title: Biometric login for mobile banking
story.description: Enable biometric login for mobile banking on supported devices using a device-bound challenge verified by the authentication service. The mobile-banking client invokes the platform biometric prompt and sends its signed result to authentication-service before receiving the existing scoped access token. Customers may opt in after a successful credential login and revoke the device registration from their session settings. Preserve the credential fallback for unsupported devices and failed prompts. Schedule the identity deployment jointly with ST-107 because both stories modify authentication-service challenge validation and cannot deploy incompatible authentication policies independently.
acceptance_criteria: An opted-in device completes a fresh signed biometric challenge before authentication-service issues the normal scoped access token.
A failed, expired or replayed biometric challenge creates no authenticated mobile banking session.
Unsupported devices retain credential login, and device revocation prevents further biometric login from that device.
ST-112 and ST-107 coordinate the authentication-service identity deployment, shared challenge contract and rollback policy to avoid a deployment collision.

requirement.business_summary: Customers using the mobile banking app on supported devices can opt in to biometric login after a successful credential login. An opted-in device must complete a fresh signed, device-bound biometric challenge that the authentication service verifies before the normal scoped access token is issued. A failed, expired or replayed challenge yields no authenticated session; unsupported devices keep credential login, and customers can revoke a device registration from session settings.
requirement.technical_summary: The mobile-banking client invokes the platform biometric prompt and submits the signed challenge result to authentication-service for validation prior to scoped access token issuance. authentication-service challenge validation is modified, and the identity deployment is scheduled jointly with ST-107 because both stories alter authentication-service challenge validation and cannot deploy incompatible authentication policies independently. A shared challenge contract and rollback policy are required to avoid a deployment collision. The existing credential fallback path and existing scoped access token flow are preserved.
affected_capabilities: Authentication challenge validation and scoped token issuance
Device registration opt-in and revocation from session settings
Credential login fallback for unsupported devices or failed prompts
Joint identity deployment, shared challenge contract and rollback policy (with ST-107)
requirement.engineering_scope: Mobile-banking client work to invoke the platform biometric prompt and transmit the signed result, plus authentication-service changes to challenge validation and device registration/revocation handling ahead of existing scoped token issuance. Credential fallback must remain intact. Delivery is coupled to ST-107 for a coordinated authentication-service identity deployment, shared challenge contract and rollback policy. Storage location and schema for device registrations, and whether any gateway or contract versioning change is needed, are not stated in the source.

findings.text: The described change is confined to a versioned English statement template layout asset in document-service, and the template selection interface and render payload contract used with reporting-service are stated to be untouched, so the personal-data exposure introduced by this change appears bounded to the existing statement rendering path rather than a new data flow. document-service and reporting-service sit upstream of authentication-service and audit-db, so publishing a new template version and approving a PDF preview involve privileged actions and traceable records.
